extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals and press-release writers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for crafting press-release headlines/subject lines that get reporters to open and readers to continue—focusing on concision, clarity about the news, and attention-grabbing word choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grab a reporter's attention / subject line importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Grabbing a reporter’s attention can all come down to your subject line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The headline/subject line is often the decisive factor in whether a reporter opens a release or pitch. Prioritize making the subject line compelling for media recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be pithy and exhaustive at the same time
rubrics_metrics.description: Guide your efforts to be pithy and exhaustive at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the headline concise (pithy) while still conveying the essential information so the reader understands the news without needing to dig—strike a balance between brevity and sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a sense of shock and awe
rubrics_metrics.description: There needs to be a sense of shock and awe as media are deluged with press releases, pitches and alerts every day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because journalists receive many messages daily, headlines that contain an element of surprise or strong newsworthiness are more likely to cut through the clutter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix 'what's the news' with catchiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that there is a mix of 'what's the news' along with a catchiness that gets the reader to go beyond the headline, sub-head and first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine clear, factual signaling of the core news with engaging phrasing so readers (and reporters) are motivated to read past the headline into the subhead and lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use words that make the reader pause (account for the 'Twitter-soundbite' world)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Twitter-soundbite-world we live in, the words used need to give the reader pause to catch up to the overall thoughts that are being conveyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose wording that stands out in short attention-span environments—use phrasing that causes a moment's pause or curiosity, rather than blending into fast-scrolling social feeds.
